Unifying Event Evolution Graphs and Reasoning
Traces via Semantic Entailment: A Dual-Phase
Architecture for Judicial GraphRAG
Md. Emam Zafor Saadik and Md. Raihan Molla
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
Bangladesh University of Business and Technology (BUBT), Dhaka, Bangladesh
Abstract—Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in law
must trace multi-hop precedent chains and must not present
overruled doctrine as current law, yet common evaluators
reward entity overlap rather than grounded reasoning. We
introduce TERRA (Temporal-Evolution and Reasoning-Trace
RAG), an experimental dual-phase GraphRAG architecture.
Offline, it builds an Event Evolution Graph over 20,000
Supreme Court opinions connected by 145,366 directed cita-
tion edges, plus a procedural reasoning-trace index. Online,
a small-model Traﬀic Cop router sends single-point lookups
down a lighter fast path (retrieval and an entailment check,
without graph traversal) and multi-hop questions through
citation traversal, and an LLM-prompted entailment grader
evaluates retrieved evidence before generation. We evaluate
on a 350-query benchmark against four baselines (1,750 eval-
uations) using two non-Llama judges, paired Wilcoxon tests
and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. TERRA scores higher
overall faithfulness (0.695 vs. 0.670 for the next best system,
overlapping 95% CIs) and answer-only faithfulness (0.586,
computed on differing answered subsets), and significantly
outperforms all three retrieval baselines on Category B multi-
hop reasoning (∆from +0.066 [HippoRAG] and +0.070 [Flat]
to +0.119 [GraphRAG]; FDR q < 0.05; Flat CI includes
zero), although a no-retrieval Direct LLM scores significantly
higher on Category B (∆= −0.081, q = 0.0023; TERRA’s
Category B faithfulness is low in absolute terms, 0.254). On
adversarial Category D queries TERRA safely handles 97.3%
of traps (64.0% explicit refusals, 33.3% verified refutations)
with 2/75 (2.7%) fatal errors, but refuses 2 Category A and
16 Category B queries, at 9.19 s median latency. On 30
obscure overruled precedents, Direct LLM safe handling falls
to 0.0% versus 63.3% for full TERRA, but TERRA without
curated overruling labels drops to 26.7%, not significantly
different from flat retrieval (p = 0.726562); safety depends
on curated annotations. Absent licensed attorney evaluation,
human review remains an essential deployment prerequisite.
Keywords—Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Lan-
guage Models, Temporal Knowledge Graph, Agentic Reason-
ing, Semantic Entailment, Explainable AI, Temporal Leakage
Evaluation
I. Introduction
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) decouples the
parametric memory of Large Language Models (LLMs)
from external knowledge bases, enabling factual grounding
and source attribution without continuous retraining. In
high-stakes settings, where errors and hallucinations carry
real consequences, the fidelity of the retrieved context is
a strict operational requirement, and naive “retrieve-then-
generate” pipelines over static vector databases and fixed-
length chunks have proven structurally inadequate.
The bottleneck arises with continuous knowledge drift
and multi-step reasoning. Static vector indices can accumu-
late conflicting, time-stamped versions of the same fact;
a retriever ranking by semantic similarity may surface
several together, leaving a frozen generator without a basis
for choosing the chronologically authoritative one and
prone to state outdated law. For multi-step derivations,
similarity-based pipelines can retrieve fragments that omit
precedential and doctrinal dependencies. We motivate the
design with these mechanisms and do not measure them
in isolation.
Recent work addresses these bottlenecks in silos. Graph-
based retrievers organize facts chronologically but lack the
procedural logic to guide multi-hop generation; retrieval
of intermediate reasoning traces improves deduction but
is temporally blind and mostly confined to mathematics
or coding; and corrective Agentic RAG frameworks rely
on retrieval evaluators that may not capture conceptual
relevance, as a SHAP-based study of the CRAG T5
evaluator found it relies mainly on named-entity alignment
rather than semantic similarity [1]. Many hybrid systems
route among a small fixed set of channels, while adaptive
multi-strategy routing is emerging [2].
We therefore introduce a dual-phase GraphRAG archi-
tecture for evolving, knowledge-intensive domains (traver-
sal stability under temporal snapshot expansion is eval-
uated in Section VI-N). All heavy computation is of-
fline, building a dual-index corpus that cross-links an
Event Evolution Graph (EEG), which encodes precedent
relationships across 20,000 judicial decisions and 145,366
directed citation edges, with a node-level procedural trace
scaffold, a fixed five-step template instantiated per case.
Online, a small language model acts as a Traﬀic Cop router
classifying each query as EASY or HARD, selecting a fast
path or citation-graph traversal, which yields a bimodal
execution profile (gross median 5.83 s on Category A
factual lookups vs. 17.94 s on Category B multi-hop
chains). Before generation, an LLM-prompted entailment
grader decides whether the retrieved evidence suﬀices; its
accuracy was not independently validated.
We compare TERRA with four baselines, including

Direct LLM and Flat Vector RAG, on a 350-query
benchmark with a 35-query pilot ablation. We did not
test attention dilution or context-length effects directly,
and TERRA’s mean retrieved context is longer than the
retrieval baselines’ (about 18,400 versus 2,900–4,100 char-
acters). In a 50-query temporal leakage probe, TERRA
did not leak less than Flat Vector RAG under default
prompting (the preregistered hypothesis H1 is not sup-
ported, and Flat RAG refused 23 of 50 queries) but gave
more historically correct answers (76.0% versus 38.0%).
The work is an experimental research framework for
context fidelity in temporal legal AI on historical SCOTUS
jurisprudence.
A. Summary of Contributions
• Dual-Index Architecture: a judicial GraphRAG cor-
pus cross-linking an EEG of 20,000 SCOTUS de-
cisions (145,366 citation edges) with a node-level
procedural trace scaffold (one five-step template per
case, with no case-specific issue, test or holding) and
no synthetic cases.
• Traﬀic

optional coarse proximity flag (dL2 < 1.3 + Ti-

and VII-B).
• NLI-Based Entailment Evaluation and XAI Attri-

• Leakage Safeguards and Audits: safeguards against
temporal precedent inversion, benchmark retrieval
contamination and cross-domain feature bleeding,
with mixed results in the leakage probe.
• Empirical Evaluation: across 1,750 evaluations (350
queries × 5 pipelines, T = 0.0) with paired Wilcoxon
tests, Cohen’s dz and 95% bootstrap CIs, TERRA has
the highest Answer-Only Faithfulness among RAG
architectures (0.586 ± 0.399 vs. HippoRAG’s 0.392 ±
0.370), outperforms Flat Vector RAG (∆= +0.070,
p = 0.0032, dz = 0.166) and HippoRAG (∆= +0.066,
p = 0.0068, dz = 0.207) on Category B, delivers
97.3% adversarial safe handling (73/75(97.3%): 48/75
(64.0%) refusals, 25/75 (33.3%) refutations) with
2/75 (2.7%) fatal errors vs. 4–8 for baselines, and
incurs 2 false refusals on Category A (16 on B). Direct
LLM scores higher on Category B (∆= −0.081),
and the Flat margin’s bootstrap CI includes zero.
Evaluations rely on automated LLM judges without
licensed attorneys, making human review an essential
prerequisite (Section VII-C).
II. Related Work
Retrieval-Augmented Generation [3], [4] decoupled para-
metric memory from external knowledge, but standard
RAG struggles with knowledge drift and multi-step rea-
soning. Graph-based architectures structure retrieved evi-
dence: GraphRAG [5] builds hierarchical entity-relation
communities for global summarization, and Think-on-
Graph [6] runs iterative LLM-guided reasoning over
knowledge graphs. In temporal domains, Liu and Cao
[7] introduced a continuous-knowledge-drift benchmark
and Chronos, a time-aware method organizing evidence
into an Event Evolution Graph (EEG); Zhang et al. [8]
proposed E2RAG for temporal-causal consistency across
entity-event subgraphs; and Zhu et al. [9] developed
STAR-RAG for time-sensitive rule graph summarization.
In law, Chen et al. [10] proposed LegalGraphRAG, a
Researcher, Auditor and Adjudicator multi-agent system
over a hierarchical legal graph, and de Martim [11]
introduced SAT-Graph RAG to trace diachronic statutory
norm versions across constitutional amendments. These
systems organize sources by abstraction level or model
formal amendment events, whereas common-law systems
also require tracking how precedent evolves across citation
networks, where earlier decisions remain presumptive
authority unless distinguished, limited or overruled; and
static graphs retrieve structure but lack the procedural
logic for multi-hop reasoning over evolving precedents.
To supply that logic, recent work augments retrieval
with intermediate reasoning trajectories. CoT-RAG [12]
combines knowledge-graph-guided chain-of-thought gener-
ation with retrieval and reports gains of 4.0% to 44.3%
across nine public reasoning datasets, and surveys of
agentic reasoning [13], [14] describe pipelines in which
agents identify knowledge gaps and generate intermedi-
ate traces to inform search. Legal benchmarks include
CaseHOLD [15], which evaluates holding identification,
and CLERC [16], which evaluates U.S. case retrieval
and analysis drafting; as we read them, neither targets
superseded or overruled authority, the gap TERRA’s
evaluation addresses. LegalBench [17] broadens coverage
to 162 tasks across six types of legal reasoning. Earlier legal
NLP work includes outcome prediction for Supreme Court
cases [18] and domain-pretrained language models such as
LEGAL-BERT [19], and an audit of leading commercial
legal research tools found that they hallucinated in more
than 17% of queries [20]. Trace-retrieval frameworks have
been evaluated mainly on quantitative domains or static
statutory collections, leaving longitudinal common-law
settings largely untested.
Query routers and evaluators form the connective tissue
of the pipeline. Hashmi [2] highlighted the rigidity of single-
channel retrieval and introduced an Adaptive Hybrid
Retrieval framework, noting that pure vector similarity
often fails to capture structural navigation. Yalavarthi
[1] found through SHAP analysis that the T5-based

evaluator in Corrective RAG (CRAG) prioritizes named-
entity matching over semantic understanding and transfers
poorly to scientific questions. Putta et al. [21] showed with
CaseFacts that unrestricted web search degrades legal fact-
checking relative to closed-book baselines. Retrievers rank-
ing by lexical or embedding similarity can return overruled
precedents alongside current ones without marking which
was overturned, which motivates the explicit entailment
check tested below.
To our knowledge, no system reviewed in Section II
unifies temporal precedent management, node-level proce-
dural trace retrieval and semantic-entailment evaluation
in one pipeline: graph models track chronology but lack
procedural logic, trace models enhance reasoning but lack
temporal awareness, and many routers select among a
few retrieval channels. TERRA cross-links a temporal
EEG with a node-level trace database, retrieving each
precedent node with its fixed five-step trace scaffold; it
uses an LLM-prompted entailment grader in place of an
entity-alignment evaluator and a binary Traﬀic Cop router
choosing between a fast path and citation-graph traversal.
This dual-phase design targets continuous knowledge drift
(examined under snapshot expansion in Section VI-N)
and multi-hop reasoning without retraining the foundation
model.
III. System Architecture and Methodology
TERRA
(Temporal-Evolution
and
Reasoning-Trace
RAG) is designed as a two-phase, closed-loop GraphRAG
architecture for temporal legal reasoning on historical
common-law jurisprudence. The core engineering philos-
ophy strictly separates offline corpus ingestion and knowl-
edge structure construction from online query routing and
inference. This separation ensures that all computationally
intensive graph traversals, citation link extractions, and
reasoning trace generations are performed offline, main-
taining responsive online inference with a bimodal latency
profile (median 5.83 s on factual lookups vs. 17.94 s on
multi-hop citation chains; Figure 1).
A. Phase 1: Offline Ingestion and Knowledge Graph Con-
struction
1) Authentic Judicial Opinion Corpus (20,000 Cases):
TERRA operates on 20,000 full-text Supreme Court opin-
ions spanning 1850–1980 (Volumes 50–448), curated from
an initial harvest of 23,010 public-domain federal decisions
from CourtListener and the Harvard Caselaw repositories
(public domain under 17 U.S.C. § 105). To remove
non-precedential noise, opinions were filtered by length
(character count ≥4,000). Of the 131,315 decisions in
399 scanned U.S. Reports volumes, 102,235 (77.85%) are
shorter than 500 characters (procedural orders, summary
dispositions and docket records, subject to audit). The
length filter nevertheless induces bias: it excludes 8,324
intermediate decisions (500–3,999 characters, 6.34%), of
which 46 rank in the top 0.5% of citation authority
under Harvard CAP PageRank (e.g., Haines v. Kerner,
Dusky v. United States, Lucas v. Earl, Sipuel v. Board
of Regents, Gayle v. Browder). The corpus contains no
synthetic cases. A core set of 34 landmark civil rights
decisions, from Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) through
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), Missouri ex rel. Gaines v.
Canada (1938) and Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
to Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg (1971), anchors the
multi-hop benchmark.
2) Citation Parsing and Directed Edge Classification:
Citations are extracted with eyecite [22], a token-level
extraction and reporter-normalization utility that estab-
lishes citation existence (A
CITES

precedential treatment or approval; strings are normalized
via cite.corrected_citation() (e.g., “347 U.S. 483”) and
matched to opinion identifier hashes. The verified Event
Evolution Graph has 145,366 directed edges (145,310
CITES and 56 OVERRULES), with forward chronological
validity at calendar-year granularity and zero cross-year
violations (0.00%); 4,077 edges (2.81%) link same-year
opinions, including 13 intra-year reporting artifacts. An
earlier “99.91% chronological validity” claim has unre-
solved provenance (likely a decimal approximation of
full-date ordering, 145, 175/145, 310 = 99.91%). A repro-
ducible stratified audit across 14 decades (N = 200, seed
20260924) confirms verbatim citation presence in 100.0%
of sampled edges (95% CI: [98.1%, 100.0%]), with 94.5%
verified direct reliance (95% CI: [90.4%, 96.9%]) and 5.5%
citations inside third-party quotations.
The OVERRULES edges are typed relations taken from
a Wikipedia mirror of the Congressional Research Service
(CRS) report R45319 and resolved to corpus nodes by cita-

replaying the current traversal code on both graphs gave
identical outputs for 159 recorded traversals, but the code
version used in the runs was not pinned. All reported
results use the frozen index; a corrected derivative with-
out the 3 edges (145,363 edges; SHA256 14827bd6...) is
released in the replication bundle as a separately versioned
file and is not used by any reported run. The 19 Category-
D queries (e.g., Brown invalidating Plessy) cover 9 distinct
OVERRULES edges, all among the 53 consistent ones
(Section V-A). The graph is serialized as a NetworkX

3) Procedural Reasoning Trace Synthesis and Vector
Serialization:
Each case is paired with a node-level
Structured Legal Reasoning Trace (SLRT), which in the
evaluated index is a fixed scaffold built from Harvard
Caselaw Access Project (CAP) metadata:
1) Curated Landmark Prototypes (N = 34): during
early development, 34 landmark decisions received
curated traces generated by instruction-tuned mod-
els (gemini-3.1-flash-lite baseline; mistral.ministral-
3-8b-instruct variants for benchmark seeds) at T =
0.0, capped at 150 words and following a five-point
schema (constitutional question, governing provi-
sions and standard of review, holding, precedent
connection, longitudinal significance). They are not
in the evaluated index.
2) Deterministic Procedural Substrate (N = 20, 000,
100.0%): all 20,000 opinions are serialized by a
procedural function (build_structured_trace) from
the CAP case title (name_abbreviation), decision
year (decision_date) and a domain phrase. Every
node receives the same five-step template (legal
question, governing precedent, factual record, harmo-
nizing doctrines, holding), with no case-specific issue,
procedural history, test or holding. The domain
phrase differs from the node’s category field for
18,247 of 20,000 nodes (19,298 read “Civil Rights
Equal Protection”, although 1,153 nodes carry that
category). The index thus holds no LLM-generated
trace text but supplies no case-specific reasoning to
the generator.

Evaluated standalone (Section VI-D), the router reaches

suite.
To limit hallucination on out-of-domain topics without
static allowlists, TERRA applies a three-layer Domain

1) Tier 1, Lexical Title Matching: checks whether q

3) Tier 3, Semantic Entailment Verification: because
proximity cannot verify authority or prevent misap-
plication, the NLI Smart Grader checks the retrieved
subgraph, and if entailment fails across two expan-
sion attempts, generation ends in a deterministic
safety refusal. In the canonical run, 81 of the 139
refusals followed an empty retrieved context (74 of
the 75 Category C probes) and 58 a non-empty one
(Section VII-B).
A fatal constraint violation is a response that aﬀirms
an overruled doctrine, misattributes controlling constitu-
tional authority or adopts a legally impossible premise
from an adversarial prompt (Category D); a false refusal is
an unwarranted refusal of an in-domain Category A lookup
whose controlling precedent is present and unambiguous.
2) Multi-Hop Citation Graph Traversal: For HARD
queries, retrieval combines vector and graph traversal.

3) NLI Smart Grader and Self-Correction Expansion
Loop: Before generation, C(q) is evaluated by the NLI
Smart Grader, a structured-prompt call to databricks-
meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct [24] (T = 0.0) given the query
and context and instructed to return JSON with entails
(boolean), confidence_score (float) and reasoning (string).
This allows single-call verification without a separate NLI
cross-encoder (e.g., DeBERTa [25]), while routing stays
with the 12B Gemma SLM. No labeled validation set
was built for the verifier; the only empirical evidence
of its role is the pilot ablation, in which removing the
gate (Ablation 2, Table II) lowers adversarial safety
rejection from 100.0% to 0.0%, which is consistent with
the gate contributing to safety but not a validation of
its accuracy. False non-entailment (insuﬀicient context
passed to the generator) is the principal unquantified
failure mode (Section VII-C). If entails == True, the
context goes to the generator. If entails == False, a Self-
Correction Expansion Loop widens retrieval (k ←k + 2),
re-queries ChromaDB and re-runs BFS. If entailment still
fails after two expansions, the Safety Refusal Firewall halts
generation with a deterministic refusal: “I apologize, but
I do not have suﬀicient validated legal context in my
databases to answer this query accurately without risking
hallucination.”
4) Data Leakage Mitigation Framework: TERRA ap-
plies four safeguards against leakage. (1) Temporal direc-
tionality: an earlier case cannot cite later jurisprudence, so
forward CITES edges require t(vcite) ≥t(vcited), and retro-
spective invalidation uses CRS-derived OVERRULES re-
lations (Section III-A) rather than unrestricted backward
edges, preventing the retriever from projecting modern
standards onto historical inquiries. (2) Vector-store iso-
lation: benchmark queries, rubrics and reference answers
are segregated from the index, which holds only opinion
text and traces. (3) Cross-domain bleed prevention: title
matching and the proximity flag (which terminated no
query in the canonical run) are coarse first-line signals,
and NLI verification is designed to suppress non-entailed

subgraphs before synthesis. (4) Temporal parametric con-
tainment: to limit post-T
doctrine entering historical
answers, traversals and retrieved corpora are bounded
by provenance timestamps (KnowledgeProvenance ≤T),
and candidate generations ˆycandidate pass an entailment
gate against contemporaneous evidence before release. In
the leakage probe (Section VI-G) the gate made six
interventions, but its bulk leakage reduction was not
statistically established.

B. Comparative Baselines
TERRA is benchmarked against four representative
baseline architectures spanning parametric and retrieval-
augmented paradigms: (1) Direct LLM (No RAG), where
query q is passed directly to the generator without
retrieval, evaluating raw parametric knowledge and un-
gated hallucination risks; (2) Flat Vector RAG, where
ChromaDB retrieves top-k reasoning traces by semantic
embedding similarity (nresults = 2) and passes them
directly to the generator without citation graph traversal
or NLI entailment grading; (3) GraphRAG-Adapted (Lou-
vain implementation), adapting Microsoft GraphRAG [5]
by partitioning opinion entities into Louvain graph com-
munities (Q = 0.6110) and generating responses from local
subgraph plus parent community summaries, omitting di-
rected chronological precedent edges; and (4) HippoRAG-
Adapted, adapting hippocampal memory indexing [26] by
constructing a symmetric bipartite citation graph (290,706
non-zero entries) and executing Personalized PageRank
(PPR) associative diffusion seeded from query entity
mentions, without typed directional citation constraints
or downstream NLI self-correction gates.

G. Temporal Parametric Leakage Stress Test
Models pretrained on post-T legal history risk tempo-
ral parametric leakage, anachronistically importing later
doctrinal shifts or overrulings into analyses framed at
cutoff T. We preregistered and ran a 50-query probe
across five horizons (T ∈{1890, 1930, 1950, 1970, 1980}),
spanning seven doctrinal domains and balanced across
case prominence and reasoning depth. Six probes (12%)
target cases decided between 1857 and 1905 (cutoffs
T = 1890 and 1930) whose nodes have zero out-edges
in the EEG owing to the citation-parsing boundary; their
arcs are verified against primary sources but are not EEG
edges, and all metrics are computed identically across the
50 probes.
1) Design, Metrics and Evaluator Reliability:
The
probe evaluates 400 responses from Direct LLM, Flat
Vector RAG, TERRAungated (Lgen) and TERRAgated
(Lfinal), each under Condition A (standard prompt) and
Condition B (explicit instruction to adhere to year T),
under a preregistered 3-tier rubric: Level 0 (clean), Level 1
(non-prejudicial mention or disclaimer) and Level 2 (fatal
reliance on post-T
law). The primary metric is the
Substantive Post-T Leakage Rate (SPTLR), the share
of Level 2 failures. Because refusing systems generate no
post-T text and look “leak-free”, we decouple containment
from problem-solving with the Refusal Rate and the
Historical Legal Correctness Rate (HLCR), whether the
system states the operative rule as of T, and we measure
the NLI Gate Leakage Interception Rate (NGLIR), the
share of ungated leaking candidates intercepted by the
gate (denominator D).
Responses were judged by qwen3-next-80b and gpt-oss-
120b. Over N = 315 complete pairs the judges reached
68.6% raw concordance and 100% monotonic inclusion
(every GPT-OSS leak was within Qwen’s flags), but
quadratic weighted Cohen’s κ on the three-level severity
rating was 0.260, lower than elsewhere (e.g., κ = 0.5746
on the obscure suite) and consistent with the Kappa

Paradox [29]: GPT-OSS rated 91.7% of responses Level 0
(289/315), inflating chance agreement to ≈60%. Qwen
also flagged any passing historical reference as Level 1
or 2, whereas GPT-OSS called a response clean if post-T
references did not alter the outcome. Evaluations were
reconciled by a pre-specified 5-tier protocol: (1) safe
refusals resolve to Level 0; (2) unanimity is preserved;
(3) lexical breach of forbidden phrases and (4) substantive
quotation of post-T law assign Level 2; (5) subtle mentions
resolve to max(s1, s2) = Level 1. Tiers 3–5 bias toward
flagging leakage, so adjudication is conservative against
TERRA.

evaluate on CaseFacts [21], a legal fact-checking dataset

1) Anti-Circularity and Graph Substrate Audit:
Of
the 20,000 nodes, exactly 34 landmark decisions (0.17%,
34/20, 000) received curated reasoning traces during early
development (not in the evaluated index), whereas the
350-query benchmark touches 284 distinct nodes (1.42%,

seed extraction is designed to anchor both extremities

was not re-audited for the canonical run, so this is
a mechanism explanation, not a measured result. For
a chain v0 →· · · →vm−1, the forward ball B(v0, 2)
covers {v0, v1, v2} and the reverse ball B(vm−1, 2) covers

beam the two neighborhoods meet at intermediate author-
ities and can cover paths of up to four hops without deeper
search. In the canonical run all gold nodes were recovered
for 16/32 4-node and 1/5 5-node chains; high fan-out
exceeding the beam is a plausible but untested explanation
for the 16 incompletely recovered 4-node chains. We did
not test causally whether TERRA’s results (Tables IV
and IX) stem from retrieval quality; Direct LLM’s higher
Category B faithfulness shows retrieval alone does not
explain faithfulness.

N. Benchmark-Graph Traversal Stability Under Temporal
Snapshot Expansion
To test traversal stability under corpus growth without
generative confounding, we run standalone breadth-first
traversal over four snapshot expansions: 1890 →1930
(Step N = 40 yr), 1930 →1950 (20 yr), 1950 →1970
(20 yr) and 1970 →1980 (10 yr). Over N = 106 qualifying
Category B observations (82 unique queries anchored at an
origin decided at or before T, with at least one later gold
authority in (T, T +N]), BFS traversal (k = 2, d = 2) was
run on G≤T and G≤T +N seeded by the origin precedent
s = q[target_nodes][0]. Grand pooled recall moved from
0.35 ± 0.13 to 0.38 ± 0.14 (∆Recall = 0.03 ± 0.16), with
90.6% of queries showing ∆Recall ≥0, a Discovery
Rate on newly eligible authorities of 0.12, and median
traversal latency under one millisecond (< 0.01 ms; mean
0.15±0.18 ms); by snapshot pair, ∆Recall is −0.10±0.25
(1890 →1930), 0.01 ± 0.15 (1930 →1950), 0.08 ± 0.14
(1950 →1970) and −0.00 ± 0.10 (1970 →1980), and the
full per-snapshot table is in the supplementary material.
Three boundaries apply: absolute recall includes the depth-
0 seed (while ∆Recall is invariant to that offset); negative
shifts stem from degree caps when expanding nodes
become hubs; and the experiment evaluates topology over
generic CITES edges on NetworkX DiGraphs, decoupled
from vector retrieval (Section VII-C) and from live index
upsert, which remains future work.
VII. Discussion
The evaluation indicates where TERRA helps (Cat-
egory B retrieval coverage, out-of-domain refusal) and
where it does not (Category B faithfulness against Direct
LLM, obscure precedents without curated labels).
A. Architectural Differentiation and System Scope
Compared with Microsoft Research’s GraphRAG [5],
which builds static hierarchical entity-relation communi-
ties for dataset summarization, TERRA models precedent
evolution through dated citation edges (CITES) and typed
OVERRULES edges imported from CRS annotations (56
tagged, 3 of them found mis-resolved on audit; the 19
Category D queries cover 9 distinct edges; Section III-A),
together with node-level reasoning traces; live updates are
untested. The NLI Smart Grader is designed to reduce
unsupported generations, although residual errors remain
[27], [30]. The offline pipeline indexes full-docket Supreme
Court jurisprudence (1850–1980) as a high-distractor
graph, while the evaluated online task is longitudinal
precedent tracking, temporal drift, and safety over con-
stitutional and federal public-law doctrine. Three design
choices distinguish TERRA, examined only in a 35-query
pilot ablation. First, domain-boundary safety pairs lexical
anchoring with downstream NLI gating and an optional,
scale-dependent geometric proximity flag that terminated
no query in the canonical run; 74 of 75 Category C
refusals followed empty retrieval. Second, entailment-gated
generation favours refusal over unsupported answers (16
of 100 Category B queries falsely refused), qualified by
the 94.5% citation-extraction precision of the underlying
graph. Third, chronological CITES edges alongside typed
OVERRULES relations let TERRA model precedent
shifts only where curated annotations exist.
B. Empirical Analysis of Firewall Component Contribu-
tions and Scale Dynamics
The design intended the Domain Boundary Firewall as
a pre-retrieval filter in which vector distance (dL2 < 1.3)
flags out-of-domain (OOD) queries. A preliminary 50-
query Category C audit on the initial 10,009-opinion
index found the gate non-functional at that scale (0/50
intercepted), since OOD distances (0.281 ≤dL2 ≤0.859)
fell entirely below 1.3. Safety in Table IV (100.0% refusal
on Category C; 64.0% refusal and 33.3% verified refutation
on Category D) was therefore delivered by downstream

refusal rather than by the proximity gate. In the canonical
run, 81 of the 139 refusals occurred on an empty retrieved
context (74 in Category C, 7 in Category D) and 58 on a
non-empty one (2, 16, 1 and 39 in Categories A–D). In the
35-query pilot ablation (Table II, Ablation 2), removing
NLI reduced adversarial safety (scored as refusal) to 0.0%
on five Category D queries, so the grader was necessary
there; the ablation does not apportion the Category C
refusals between empty-context and entailment-based re-
fusal.
On the 20,000-opinion corpus (Table XII, Panel B), the
full N = 75 Category C suite gives an isolated AUROC
of 0.9901. At τ = 1.30, offline calibration gives 0.00% in-
domain false refusal (0/200) and flags 54.67% (41/75) of
the OOD probes by distance; the deployed run terminated
no query before retrieval. That 50/50 probes fell below
1.3 on the 10k index while 41/75 exceed it on the 20k
index is consistent with density effects as the corpus grows
across seven constitutional domains, but two snapshots do
not support a scaling law. We therefore treat geometric
proximity only as an optional coarse pre-filter that could
save compute on obvious outliers.
C. Limitations
We state the essential limitations here; narrower caveats
are noted where the corresponding results are reported.
1) No licensed-practitioner evaluation. All faithfulness
and safety scores come from automated LLM judges
and ROUGE-L against researcher-constructed refer-
ences, and cannot replicate practitioner judgment of
legal correctness, temporal consistency or citation va-
lidity; 880 of the 1,750 canonical evaluations (50.3%)
score exactly 1.0, which limits discrimination among
high-scoring systems. The NLI Smart Grader has
no labelled validation set, so its false-non-entailment
rate is unquantified beyond ablation evidence, and
the author spot-check in Section VI-H is a single non-
expert review. Expert evaluation is a prerequisite for
deployment.
2) Shared model family. Generation, NLI grading and
the Category D verifier, which produces the re-
fusal, refutation, fatal-error and hedge labels, all
use databricks-meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct, whereas
the two faithfulness judges are from other families;
Category D labels may therefore inherit shared
Llama biases, and a cross-family verifier ablation
has not been run.
3) Safety depends on curated labels. Full TERRA’s
advantage on obscure overruled precedents is contin-
gent on curated OVERRULES annotations, which
carry a relation tag and a larger excerpt budget,
and the obscure pairs were drawn from these edges;
the bundled ablation cannot isolate the tag, the suite
has thirty items, and judges were not fully blind to
arm identity. Three of the 56 tagged edges were also
found mis-resolved on audit (Section III-A); none
was serialised in a deployed context, but indirect
effects are not excluded.
D. Future Work
Future research will: (1) conduct licensed practitioner
evaluation across the 350-query benchmark; (2) scale
corpus ingestion to the full federal repository; and (3) cod-
ify OVERRULES annotations as explicit weighted graph
edges with adaptive invalidation-path traversal.
VIII. Conclusion
This paper introduced TERRA, an experimental dual-
phase GraphRAG architecture addressing knowledge drift
and multi-step legal reasoning on historical SCOTUS ju-
risprudence (1850–1980). Structuring 20,000 authentic de-
cisions (145,366 citation edges) with procedural reasoning
traces, TERRA enables inference via Traﬀic Cop routing,
BFS traversal, and an NLI grader evaluating retrieved
evidence. Benchmarking across 350 queries (1,750 evalu-
ations) shows higher Category B multi-hop faithfulness
than Flat Vector RAG, HippoRAG, and GraphRAG (∆
from +0.066 to +0.119; q < 0.05; the paired interval
against Flat includes zero), though not over Direct LLM
(−0.081); higher overall faithfulness (0.695 vs. 0.670, over-
lapping CIs; 0.586); and 97.3% adversarial safe handling
(48/75(64.0%) refusals, 25/75 (33.3%) refutations). Con-
straints include 2/75 (2.7%) fatal errors, false refusals on
2 Category A and 16 Category B queries, and reliance
on curated overruling annotations (Section VI-H). Criti-
cally, because evaluations rely on automated LLM judges
without licensed attorneys (Section VII-C), human expert
review remains an essential prerequisite for deployment. In
a standalone traversal test over four snapshot expansions,
pooled recall shifted by 0.03 ± 0.16 (Section VI-N).
